newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Grenade blast wounds 33 in Addis Ababa supermarket.
newsitem.headline: Grenade blast wounds 33 in Addis Ababa supermarket.

text.p: A hand grenade exploded in a large Addis Ababa supermarket on Monday, wounding 33 people in the third such attack in the Ethiopian capital in three days, police said.
In a statement, police said the grenade was lobbed on Monday into the Tana supermarket in the Ethiopian capital's Merkato main market area. It said all casualties were taken to hospital.
The attack took place at about 5 p.m. (1400 GMT) when the supermarket is usually bustling with shoppers after work.
Police advised the public to be on alert to avoid "terrorist" attacks and said they were searching for the attackers. The supermarket was state-owned until it was sold to a businessman last year.
Following the blast, the supermarket, one of the most modern and largest in Addis Ababa, was cordoned off by police units.
It was the latest in a series of apparently politically motivated bombings in Addis Ababa and provincial cities.
Grenade blasts in an Italian restaurant and a hotel in the capital on Saturday killed an Ethiopian waitress and wounded a total of 42 people including four Britons and a French couple.
Diplomats said earlier on Monday that a French couple who were wounded in one of the two blasts in Addis Ababa on Saturday had been evacuated by plane to Paris for treatment.
Two Britons who were also injured in an attack on the chic Blue Tops restaurant in the capital were expected to be flown home to Britain for treatment later on Monday, doctors said.
The two British men said they were in Ethiopia to train the police and threw themselves at one of the grenades to protect their wives at the restaurant, favoured by foreigners and rich Ethiopians.
A doctor at the Russian-run Baltcha Hospital in Addis Ababa said on Monday the French woman was injured in one of her eyes and the French man had been wounded by shrapnel in his legs.
Ethiopian police said a waitress died and 33 people were wounded when a grenade was lobbed into the Tigray Hotel near the busy Piazza area in the city centre, at about the same time.

Diplomats said they had unconfirmed reports of at least two more grenade attacks in Addis Ababa on Saturday night but one failed to explode. One of the alleged targets -- the Meridien Hotel on Bole Road -- was unscathed.
Britons John Bown and Blair Davies told Reuters in the Black Lion hospital that as they sat down to dine, they saw something that looked like an explosive device lobbed near their table.
"We instinctively threw ourselves on the explosive to protect our wives from serious injuries," Bown said. "Thank god our wives escaped with light injuries, while we suffered multiple lacerations."
President Meles Zenawi's government blamed Moslem fundamentalists for several bomb attacks last year. Ethiopian authorities remain secretive about their investigations.

British, French and German tourists were wounded last February in a grenade attack on a hotel in the ancient walled city of Harar in the east. Last November, hijackers believed to be Ethiopians seized an Ethiopian Airlines plane and forced it to ditch off the Comoro Islands, killing 125 people on board.

Last August Ethiopian troops backed by the air force raided alleged Moslem fundamentalist bases in western Somalia and the al-Ittihad al-Islam (Islamic Unity) party said it would revenge the incursion.

The government has bad relations with neighbouring Sudan and accused Khartoum of helping plot a failed attempt to assassinate Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak when he visited Addis Ababa in June 1995.
